topic.title: The HALEU Gap: Is a Nuclear-Fuel Enrichment Bottleneck the Sleeper Constraint on AI's Advanced-Reactor Power Bet?
topic.trigger: On September 9, 2026, Centrus Energy -- the sole US company with an operating commercial-scale High-Assay Low-Enriched Uranium (HALEU) enrichment cascade -- signed a HALEU supply contract with microreactor developer Radiant that includes customer prepayments to help fund capacity expansion, with supply beginning before the end of the decade. This follows a run of 2026 disclosures no prior report in this pipeline has examined: DOE's January 2026 award of $2.7 billion to three enrichment companies (Centrus, General Matter, Orano Federal Services); Centrus completing a 900-kilogram HALEU demonstration milestone in mid-June 2026 and transitioning its cascade to commercial operation on July 1, 2026; General Matter breaking ground in August 2026 on a $1.5 billion Paducah, Kentucky enrichment facility; and continued reporting that HALEU scarcity has already forced at least a three-year schedule slip in TerraPower's Natrium reactor -- even as Meta, Google, Amazon and Microsoft have collectively committed to more nuclear power for AI data centers in the last 18 months than the US signed in the previous twenty years, much of it contingent on HALEU-fueled advanced reactor designs.

questions.primary: Is the shortage of High-Assay Low-Enriched Uranium (HALEU) -- the specialized nuclear fuel required by nearly every advanced reactor design hyperscalers have contracted for -- a genuine structural bottleneck constraining AI data centers' nuclear power bet, or a future-dated risk that does not yet touch the AI buildout actually under construction?
sub: How concentrated is HALEU enrichment capacity today, and how do DOE's $2.7 billion award and the Centrus-Radiant contract change the supply timeline?

Which hyperscaler-backed reactor designs (Oklo Aurora, TerraPower Natrium, X-energy Xe-100, Kairos KP-FHR) actually require HALEU, versus which current AI-linked nuclear deals (Three Mile Island restart, Vistra uprates) use conventional fuel unaffected by the shortage?
What concrete evidence exists that HALEU unavailability has already delayed a reactor project, and does that delay reach AI data centers counting on that power?
How does the 2028 Russian uranium import ban interact with the HALEU shortage, and what new capacity is coming online before then?
Do credible forecasts show HALEU demand overtaking realistic supply expansion before the 2030-2035 window hyperscalers have targeted for these reactors?

thesis: High-Assay Low-Enriched Uranium (HALEU) -- the 5%-to-20%-enriched nuclear fuel required by nearly every advanced reactor design hyperscalers have contracted for (Oklo's Aurora, TerraPower's Natrium, X-energy's Xe-100, Kairos Power's KP-FHR) -- meets the strict Structural Bottleneck test at the enrichment layer itself: extreme, NDAA-mandated demand growth; low near-term supply elasticity (a single small US commercial producer, Centrus Energy, with new capacity not due before 2029, after a 2024 law banned the historically dominant Russian supplier); and hard substitutability, since these reactor cores cannot run on conventional low-enriched uranium. But the AI industry's actual nearest-term nuclear power additions -- Constellation's Three Mile Island restart for Microsoft and Vistra's existing-plant capacity contracted to Meta, both targeted online by 2027 -- use conventional fuel entirely unaffected by this constraint, so the bottleneck currently gates a 2028-2035 advanced-reactor bet, not the AI buildout actually under construction. A well-capitalized three-way capacity race (Centrus, General Matter, Urenco), backed by $2.7 billion in DOE awards, is already underway on roughly the same timeline the hyperscaler-backed reactors need fuel, making this a genuine but still-latent bottleneck worth continued validation rather than a proven current constraint.

facts.statement: In January 2026 the US Department of Energy awarded $2.7 billion over ten years to three companies to strengthen domestic uranium enrichment: American Centrifuge Operating (Centrus) and General Matter each received a $900 million task order to build domestic HALEU enrichment capacity, while Orano Federal Services received $900 million to expand conventional low-enriched uranium (LEU) capacity.

Centrus completed production of the final 900 kilograms of HALEU required under its prior DOE demonstration contract in mid-June 2026, two weeks ahead of schedule, then intends to privately operate its existing American Centrifuge Plant (Piketon, Ohio) cascade on a commercial basis starting July 1, 2026, while building new capacity -- an initial build-out of 12 metric tons of annual HALEU production, with first new capacity expected online by 2029 -- under a separate fixed-price contract with a total value reported at $1.07 billion.

On September 9, 2026, Centrus signed a HALEU supply contract with microreactor developer Radiant that includes prepayments from Radiant to help fund Centrus's commercial enrichment capacity expansion, with Centrus intending to begin supplying the fuel before the end of the decade.

General Matter, a uranium-enrichment startup founded in 2024 that has not yet operated any enrichment facility or publicly disclosed its enrichment technology, received a $900 million DOE task order in January 2026 and broke ground in August 2026 on a reported $1.5 billion enrichment facility at the former Paducah Gaseous Diffusion Plant site in Kentucky, targeting the start of enrichment operations in 2034; its CEO said the plant could eventually satisfy 'all domestic demand' for HALEU by the early 2030s.

The Prohibiting Russian Uranium Imports Act, signed into law May 13, 2024, bans Russian uranium imports outright starting January 1, 2028, with interim annual waiver quotas declining from 476,536 kilograms in 2024 to 459,083 kilograms in 2027; Rosatom subsidiary TENEX -- historically the world's only commercial HALEU supplier -- separately rescinded its general license to export material to the US, effective through December 31, 2025, requiring specific export licenses for any remaining shipments.
Before the 2024 ban took effect, Rosatom was estimated to control roughly 44% of global uranium enrichment capacity and to have supplied nearly 25% of the enriched uranium used by US utilities.

TerraPower's Natrium demonstration reactor at Kemmerer, Wyoming was delayed by at least two years from its original 2028 in-service target after Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine eliminated what was then the only available commercial HALEU source; the target has since slipped further, with the project's completion date moving from 2028 to 2030 and, most recently, TerraPower's own COO citing 2031 for commercial power on the grid, under a long-term HALEU supply agreement covering up to 150 metric tons from 2028 through 2037.

Meta announced agreements on January 9, 2026 for up to 6.6 gigawatts of nuclear power: 2.6 GW (including 433 MW of new uprates) from Vistra's existing, conventionally fueled Ohio and Pennsylvania plants; up to 1.2 GW from an Oklo 'Aurora Powerhouse' reactor campus planned for Pike County, Ohio, by 2034; and up to eight TerraPower Natrium units providing 2.8 GW of baseload power plus 1.2 GW of integrated storage.

Google and Kairos Power signed a Master Plant Development Agreement on October 14, 2024 to deploy up to 500 MW of Kairos's fluoride-salt-cooled, HALEU-fueled KP-FHR advanced reactors by 2035, with a first plant targeted in Tennessee, in partnership with the Tennessee Valley Authority, around 2030.

Amazon's Climate Pledge Fund led X-energy's initial $500 million capital raise in October 2024 to support deployment of up to 12 HALEU-fueled Xe-100 high-temperature gas reactors at a Washington state project; separately, Amazon signed a large (reported at over $20 billion) agreement tied to Talen Energy's existing, conventionally fueled Susquehanna nuclear plant in Pennsylvania.

Microsoft signed a 20-year power purchase agreement with Constellation Energy, announced September 20, 2024, to restart Three Mile Island Unit 1 -- an existing Babcock & Wilcox pressurized-water reactor renamed the Crane Clean Energy Center -- targeting power delivery in 2027, one year ahead of the plant's original 2028 restart schedule.

The FY2024 National Defense Authorization Act directed DOE to make at least 21 metric tons of HALEU available to advanced reactor developers by June 2026; five companies -- Kairos Power, Radiant, Westinghouse, TerraPower, and X-energy subsidiary TRISO-X -- met DOE's prioritization criteria for early deliveries under the resulting HALEU Availability Program.

Government and industry forecasts of 2030 HALEU demand diverge sharply: DOE has cited a need for more than 40 metric tons per year, while a separate, Nuclear Energy Institute-linked estimate projects cumulative demand ramping from 2.8 metric tons in 2021 to more than 400 metric tons by 2030; sources agree that nine of the ten advanced reactor designs the US government has funded require HALEU rather than conventional low-enriched uranium.

Urenco is designing a HALEU production line at its Capenhurst, UK Advanced Fuels facility targeting up to 27 tonnes of HALEU per year, a project supported by the UK government since 2024 with a modular design allowing further expansion; separately, in June 2026 Urenco announced a nearly 50% expansion of its existing US low-enriched-uranium (not HALEU) capacity, adding 2.1 million separative work units via up to 24 new centrifuge cascades, with the first new cascades starting production in 2032 and additional cascades through 2036.

Centrus Energy (NYSE: LEU) reported Q2 2026 (period ended June 30, 2026) revenue of $176.1 million (+14% year over year) and trailing-twelve-month revenue of $452.3 million; its market capitalization was approximately $3.1-3.2 billion as of mid-September 2026, with its stock down from a 52-week high of $464.25 to $152.31.

Oklo Inc. (NYSE: OKLO) reported its first-ever quarterly revenue of $1.2 million in Q2 2026, characterized as acquisition-related rather than commercial reactor or power-sale revenue; its market capitalization was approximately $8.1 billion as of September 2026, and analysts project revenue rising from $7.9 million in 2027 to $53.3 million in 2028, well before its first commercial Aurora Powerhouse unit -- targeted for Idaho in 2027 -- is expected to be generating meaningful sales.

inferences.statement: Because the largest AI-linked nuclear power commitments actually under construction or restart through 2027-2028 -- Constellation's Three Mile Island Unit 1 restart for Microsoft and the 2.6 GW of existing Vistra capacity Meta contracted -- rely on conventional, sub-5%-enriched uranium fuel used by standard pressurized/boiling-water reactor designs rather than HALEU, the current HALEU supply constraint does not bind the AI buildout's nearest-term nuclear power additions.

Because every hyperscaler-backed advanced-reactor design with a HALEU dependency (Oklo Aurora, TerraPower Natrium, X-energy Xe-100, Kairos KP-FHR) targets first commercial operation between 2027 and 2035, and TerraPower's own experience shows a HALEU-driven slip from 2028 to 2031, the HALEU bottleneck's demonstrated effect to date has been to push these specific projects' timelines later rather than to constrain AI compute capacity hyperscalers have already committed to bringing online through 2028.

Because US commercial HALEU enrichment capacity is currently confined to a single small-scale operating cascade (Centrus, roughly 900 kilograms produced over a multi-year demonstration contract) with new 12-metric-ton-per-year capacity not expected before 2029, while government and industry demand estimates for 2030 range from roughly 40 to over 400 metric tons per year, near-term US domestic HALEU supply appears very likely to fall short of even the low end of stated 2030 demand despite DOE's $2.7 billion program and the new Centrus-Radiant contract.

Because three separate entities (Centrus, General Matter, and Urenco) are now racing to add HALEU or HALEU-adjacent enrichment capacity with substantial government backing, and General Matter's and Urenco's expansions do not depend on Centrus's already-demonstrated centrifuge technology succeeding, the HALEU bottleneck is better characterized as a capacity-buildout timing problem attracting an active, well-funded capital response than as a bottleneck with no visible supply-side remedy.

Because General Matter has received a $900 million government award and broken ground on a facility despite not having operated any enrichment facility or disclosed its enrichment technology, credible near-term (pre-2029) US HALEU supply growth is more concentrated in Centrus's already-demonstrated centrifuge technology than the headline three-company capacity buildout suggests.

unknowns: No source found discloses whether Amazon's Xe-100 project in Washington state, or any other announced advanced-reactor project, has secured a confirmed, contracted HALEU supply volume beyond the DOE HALEU Availability Program's initial small-scale allocations, making it unclear how much of the 40-400 metric ton 2030 demand forecast already has fuel commitments versus none.

The precise reconciliation between DOE's '>40 metric tons/year by 2030' figure and the Nuclear Energy Institute-linked '>400 metric tons cumulative by 2030' figure was not found in any source gathered; it is unclear whether these measure different things (annual run-rate versus cumulative fuel loaded) or reflect genuinely divergent forecasts.

Whether TerraPower's Kemmerer 1 project -- now targeting 2031 -- will actually receive its full 150-metric-ton, 2028-2037 HALEU supply on schedule from a still-not-yet-expanded Centrus/General Matter/Urenco capacity base was not confirmed by any source gathered.

No source found quantifies what share, if any, of AI hyperscaler capital committed to advanced-reactor deals (Meta, Google, Amazon) is contingent on, or could be redirected because of, continued HALEU unavailability.

All primary-source domains attempted (energy.gov, sec.gov, centrusenergy.com, about.fb.com, blog.google, x-energy.com, urenco.com, world-nuclear-news.org, utilitydive.com, nucnet.org) were blocked by the research environment's egress proxy; facts rely on convergent search-result snippets and secondary reprints rather than directly retrieved primary-source text.

industry_chain.name: Advanced reactor fuel fabrication and reactor OEMs

bottlenecks.rationale: Meets all three strict criteria: demand growth is Extreme, driven by an NDAA mandate and multi-gigawatt hyperscaler reactor commitments; supply elasticity is Low, with a single small operating US source and new capacity multiple years out after the historic Russian supplier was banned by law; substitutability is Hard, since advanced-reactor cores are engineered specifically for 5-20% enrichment and cannot run on conventional LEU.

bottlenecks.node: Near-term (2026-2028) AI data-center nuclear/grid power capacity actually under construction
bottlenecks.expansion_time: 1-3 years (existing-plant restarts and uprates, gas turbines, grid power)
bottlenecks.rationale: The AI buildout's actual near-term nuclear capacity additions -- the Three Mile Island restart and Vistra uprates -- use conventional fuel unaffected by the HALEU constraint, and hyperscalers can also draw on gas turbines and grid power (examined in this pipeline's prior transformer and PJM reports). This layer is not exposed to the HALEU bottleneck.

bottlenecks.node: Hyperscaler-committed advanced-reactor pipeline (Oklo, TerraPower Natrium, X-energy Xe-100, Kairos KP-FHR) targeting 2027-2035
bottlenecks.expansion_time: Long lead: both reactor construction and fuel-supply capacity are measured in years
bottlenecks.rationale: Demand is Extreme and HALEU substitutability is Hard, but the bottleneck's supply elasticity is being actively addressed by a well-funded, multi-company capacity build-out (DOE's $2.7 billion program, Centrus's 12-metric-ton/year expansion, General Matter, Urenco) timed to roughly match this layer's own multi-year deployment schedule. Classified as Growth Area rather than a separately confirmed Structural Bottleneck, since the strict classification is reserved for the upstream enrichment-capacity node above.

General Matter's progress at its Paducah, Kentucky facility, including any disclosed enrichment technology or licensing milestone

Further DOE HALEU Availability Program allocations or new task orders
Urenco's Capenhurst HALEU line reaching a final investment decision

bear_case.argument: The AI buildout's largest and nearest-term nuclear power additions -- Constellation's Three Mile Island Unit 1 restart and Vistra's 2.6 GW of existing-plant capacity contracted to Meta -- run on conventional, sub-5%-enriched fuel and are entirely unaffected by the HALEU shortage, meaning the bottleneck does not touch the AI power capacity hyperscalers are actually bringing online through 2027-2028.

Three separate entities (Centrus, General Matter, and Urenco) are now building new HALEU or HALEU-adjacent capacity with a combined multi-billion-dollar government backing, indicating the constraint is attracting an active, well-capitalized supply response rather than being structurally unaddressed.

General Matter, one of two companies given a $900 million DOE HALEU task order, has never operated an enrichment facility and has not disclosed the enrichment technology it plans to use, adding execution uncertainty to a meaningful share of the government's own capacity-expansion plan.

Hyperscaler-backed HALEU-dependent reactor projects (Oklo, TerraPower Natrium, X-energy Xe-100, Kairos KP-FHR) are all still pre-commercial, with first units targeted between 2027 and 2035; Oklo's own Q2 2026 revenue of $1.2 million shows how far these projects remain from operating at a scale that fuel availability could actually constrain today.

Published 2030 HALEU demand forecasts disagree by roughly an order of magnitude (approximately 40 to over 400 metric tons per year), undermining confidence in exactly how large a supply-demand gap exists to plan capacity against.

kill_conditions.condition: New commercial HALEU capacity (Centrus's expansion, General Matter, or Urenco's Capenhurst line) comes online meaningfully ahead of the 2029-2032 targets currently disclosed
kill_conditions.metric: Confirmed first commercial HALEU output date at any of the three producers
kill_conditions.threshold: Commercial-scale output confirmed at least 12 months ahead of the producer's own disclosed target

kill_conditions.condition: A hyperscaler or reactor developer discloses that a near-term (pre-2028), already-under-construction AI power project is delayed specifically due to HALEU unavailability
kill_conditions.metric: Public disclosure naming HALEU as the delay cause for a project targeted before 2028

kill_conditions.condition: Government and industry HALEU 2030 demand forecasts converge toward the lower end of the current 40-400 metric-ton range and confirm planned new capacity is sufficient to meet it
kill_conditions.metric: A reconciled DOE/NEI/industry 2030 HALEU demand-versus-supply forecast
kill_conditions.threshold: A published, reconciled forecast showing supply meeting or exceeding demand by 2030

kill_conditions.condition: General Matter's Paducah facility or another DOE-backed HALEU capacity award is delayed, cancelled, or defunded
kill_conditions.metric: Public disclosure of award cancellation, funding withdrawal, or a confirmed multi-year delay
kill_conditions.threshold: At least one confirmed cancellation, defunding, or delay of 2+ years beyond the disclosed target
